'''Paraskevas Andreas Sphicas''' {{post-nominals|FRS}} ({{langx|el|Παρασκευάς Σφήκας}}) is a [[Particle physics|particle physicist]]<ref name=gs/> who focuses on studies of [[High energy nuclear physics|High energy]] collisions in the [[Large Hadron Collider]] through which he explores [[supersymmetry]] and the mechanism of [[spontaneous symmetry breaking]]. He is a senior scientist at [[CERN]] and professor of physics at the [[National and Kapodistrian University of Athens]]. He was elected  a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] (FRS) in 2019.<ref name=frs>{{Cite web|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/paraskevas-sphicas-14126/|website=royalsociety.org|author=Anon|year=2019|language=en|access-date=2019-04-20|title=Professor Paraskevas Sphicas FRS}} One or more of the preceding sentences incorporates text from the royalsociety.org website where: {{blockquote|“All text published under the heading 'Biography' on Fellow profile pages is available under [[Creative Commons license|Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License]].” --{{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161111170346/https://royalsociety.org/about-us/terms-conditions-policies/|title=Royal Society Terms, conditions and policies|date=2016-11-11}}}}</ref>

==Education==
Sphicas received his [[Bachelor of Science]]<ref name=sb>{{cite thesis|degree=BS|last=Sphicas|first=Paraskevas Andreas|website=mit.edu|url= http://library.mit.edu/item/000212538|title=Reconstruction of the B particle vertex, a Monte-Carlo simulation of the time expansion chamber|oclc=11959937 |year=1984|publisher=Massachusetts Institute of Technology}}</ref> and [[PhD]]<ref name=phd>{{cite thesis|degree=Phd|last=Sphicas|first=Paraskevas Andreas|website=mit.edu|url=http://library.mit.edu/item/000371225|year=1988|title=Search for a high-mass resonance decaying to jets in proton-antiproton collisions|oclc=19227563|publisher=Massachusetts Institute of Technology}}</ref> degrees in physics from the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in 1984 and 1988 respectively.<ref name="iasa">{{Cite web|url=http://www.iasa.gr/people/sphicas/index_en.html|title=People Directory, Institute of Accelerating Systems and Applications, Athens, Greece|website=iasa.gr|language=en|access-date=2019-04-20}}</ref> Sphicas worked on his PhD thesis at the [[UA1 experiment]] in [[CERN]], looking for new [[Resonance (particle physics)|resonances]] that decay into [[Jet (particle physics)|jets]] and studying the production of multiple particle jets.

== Career and research ==
After obtaining his doctorate, he continued at CERN, researching [[Top quark|top]] and [[Bottom quark|bottom]] quarks. He moved back to the US in 1990 when appointed a Wilson Fellow by [[Fermilab]].<ref name="fermilab">{{Cite web|url=http://www.fnal.gov/pub/forphysicists/fellowships/robert_wilson/past.html|title=Past Wilson Fellows|website=fnal.gov|language=en|access-date=2019-04-20}}</ref> He worked on the [[Tevatron]] at the [[Collider Detector at Fermilab]] (CDF). In 1991, he joined the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT), becoming associate professor in 1994 and then Professor in 1997.<ref name=frs/>

Sphicas continued work on the CDF through the 1990s as part of MIT's team in the CDF experiments. The MIT Team was responsible for three Collider components: the forward calorimeter, the [[Data acquisition|Data Acquisition System]] and the Third Level Trigger. The 18 MIT scientists, by then led by Sphicas, were part of the team that produced the first evidence for the [[Top quark]] in 1994.<ref name="mitquark">{{Cite web|url=https://news.mit.edu/1994/quark-0427|title=MITers help discover evidence of top quark|website=news.mit.edu|date=27 April 1994 |language=en|access-date=2019-04-20}}</ref>

Sphicas began participating in the [[Compact Muon Solenoid]] (CMS) experiment at CERN in 1994. His early contributions included the development of the Data Acquisition System and the High Level Trigger for CMS, and also the setting up of the Physics Reconstruction and Selection division. In 2002, he moved from MIT to CERN to focus on the CMS. He was also appointed as Professor of Physics at the [[National and Kapodistrian University of Athens]] in 2002. He worked in several supervisory roles in the CMS experiment, as it progressed towards the discovery of the [[Higgs boson]] in 2012. He co-chaired the publication committee of the experiment in 2012-13 and was then appointed deputy spokesperson for the experiment for three years beginning in 2014.

Sphicas is currently working on the upgrade of the level-1 trigger system of the CMS, preparing for the [[High Luminosity Large Hadron Collider|High Luminosity phase of the Large Hadron Collider]] at CERN, set to complete by 2026. He has also been serving as the chair of European Committee for Future Accelerators since January 2024.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://ecfa.web.cern.ch/plenary-ecfa-composition | title = Plenary ECFA Composition | access-date = 26 May 2024}}</ref>
